enonce_markdown: A bus covers $180\,\mathrm{km}$ in $2.5$ hours at a steady speed. Its speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Speed $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. For an answer in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, express the distance in metres and the time in seconds (or divide a speed in $\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ by $3.6$).

### Solution

Distance: $180\,\mathrm{km} = 180\,000\,\mathrm{m}$. Time: $2.5\,\mathrm{h} = 2.5 \times 3\,600 = 9\,000\,\mathrm{s}$.

$v = \dfrac{180\,000}{9\,000} = 20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (which is $72\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$).

$72$ is the speed in $\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$, not converted; $1.2$ divides by $60$ instead of $3.6$; $450$ multiplies distance by time. **Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown: A train slows down uniformly from $90\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ to $54\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ in $10\,\mathrm{s}$. The size of its deceleration is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Acceleration $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$, with the speeds in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (divide $\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ by $3.6$). A negative value means a deceleration.

### Solution

$u = \dfrac{90}{3.6} = 25\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $v = \dfrac{54}{3.6} = 15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$a = \dfrac{15 - 25}{10} = -1.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so the deceleration is $1.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

$3.6$ uses the change of speed in $\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ ($36/10$) without converting; $2.5$ and $1.5$ divide the initial or the final speed alone by the time. **Answer: a.**

enonce_markdown: A car travelling at $20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ brakes and slows down uniformly at $5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ until it stops. The distance it travels while braking is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

For uniformly accelerated motion, $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$. The car stops, so the final speed is $v = 0$; the acceleration is negative because the car slows down.

### Solution

$0 = 20^{2} + 2 \times (-5) \times s \Rightarrow 10\,s = 400 \Rightarrow s = 40\,\mathrm{m}$.

$4$ is the braking time $u/a$ in seconds, not a distance; $80$ forgets the factor $2$ in $2as$; $100$ multiplies $u$ by $a$. **Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown:
The speed $v$ of a toy car moving along a straight track was read at intervals of $2\,\mathrm{s}$:

| $t$ / s | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $v$ / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 0 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 0 |

Between consecutive readings, the speed changes at a steady rate. The average speed of the toy car over the whole $10\,\mathrm{s}$ is:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The distance travelled is the area under the speed-time graph. Average speed $= \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$. Split the motion into stages of constant acceleration.

### Solution

From $0$ to $2\,\mathrm{s}$ (uniform acceleration): distance $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10 = 10\,\mathrm{m}$.

From $2$ to $8\,\mathrm{s}$ (constant speed): distance $= 6 \times 10 = 60\,\mathrm{m}$.

From $8$ to $10\,\mathrm{s}$ (uniform deceleration to rest): distance $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 10 = 10\,\mathrm{m}$.

Total distance $= 10 + 60 + 10 = 80\,\mathrm{m}$, so the average speed is $\dfrac{80}{10} = 8.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$5.0$ is the mean of $0$ and $10$ (it ignores the time spent at the top speed); $6.0$ counts only the steady stretch ($60/10$); $10$ is the maximum speed. **Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown:
A student releases a trolley on a long runway and a sensor records its speed $v$ every second:

| $t$ / s | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $v$ / $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ | 2 | 5 | 8 | 11 | 14 |

(i) Show from the table that the acceleration is constant, and calculate its value. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Calculate the distance travelled by the trolley in the $4\,\mathrm{s}$. *[3 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Acceleration is the change of speed per second, $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$. For uniform acceleration, $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2}$, or $s = $ average speed $\times$ time.

### Solution

(i) The speed increases by $3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ every second ($5-2$, $8-5$, $11-8$, $14-11$), so the acceleration is constant: $a = \dfrac{14 - 2}{4} = 3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(ii) $u = 2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $a = 3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $t = 4\,\mathrm{s}$:

$s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2} = 2 \times 4 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 4^{2} = 8 + 24 = 32\,\mathrm{m}$.

Check with the average speed: $\dfrac{2 + 14}{2} \times 4 = 8 \times 4 = 32\,\mathrm{m}$.

enonce_markdown:
A boy standing on level ground throws a ball vertically upwards at $20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Ignore air resistance and take $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(i) Calculate the maximum height reached and the time taken to reach it. *[3 marks]*

(ii) Calculate the speed of the ball when it first passes a point $15\,\mathrm{m}$ above the ground. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Calculate the time that passes between the two moments when the ball is at the height of $15\,\mathrm{m}$ (going up, then coming down). *[3 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

On the way up, the ball decelerates at $g$: use $v = u - gt$ and $v^{2} = u^{2} - 2gh$ (upwards positive). At the top the speed is momentarily zero.

### Solution

(i) At the top $v = 0$: $0 = 20^{2} - 2 \times 10 \times H \Rightarrow H = \dfrac{400}{20} = 20\,\mathrm{m}$.

$0 = 20 - 10t \Rightarrow t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$.

(ii) $v^{2} = 20^{2} - 2 \times 10 \times 15 = 400 - 300 = 100 \Rightarrow v = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (upwards).

(iii) Going up, $v = 20 - 10t = 10 \Rightarrow t_1 = 1\,\mathrm{s}$. By symmetry the ball returns to $15\,\mathrm{m}$ with the same speed, $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ downwards, so $v = 20 - 10t = -10 \Rightarrow t_2 = 3\,\mathrm{s}$. (Check with $s = ut - 5t^{2}$: $20 - 5 = 15$ at $t = 1$, and $60 - 45 = 15$ at $t = 3$.)

Time between the two passages: $3 - 1 = 2\,\mathrm{s}$.
